title: Paper I · B. Constitution, Polity, Social Justice & IR › B1: Indian Constitution: Evolution, features, Preamble, Fundamental Rights, Fundamental Duties, Directive Principles of State Policy, Amendments, Significant Provisions and Basic Structure.

official_questions.stem: The Supreme Court of Bengal was constituted by the-Crown in the year

statements.t: The Supreme Court of Bengal was constituted by the Crown in 1776.
statements.fact: 1776 is wrong. Correct: The Supreme Court of Bengal was constituted by the Crown in 1774.

statements.t: The Supreme Court of Bengal was constituted by the Crown in 1777.
statements.fact: 1777 is wrong. Correct: The Supreme Court of Bengal was constituted by the Crown in 1774.

statements.t: The Supreme Court of Bengal was constituted by the Crown in 1774.

official_questions.stem: The State takes steps to organize Village Panchayats as per the Constitution of India under
official_questions.core_fact: Article 40 (DPSP, Gandhian principle) directs the State to organise village panchayats and endow them with powers to function as units of self-government.

statements.t: The State takes steps to organise village panchayats under Article 39 of the Constitution.
statements.fact: Article 39 lists principles of policy (livelihood, distribution of resources, equal pay, children); panchayats are Article 40.

statements.t: The State takes steps to organise village panchayats under Article 41 of the Constitution.
statements.fact: Article 41 = right to work, education and public assistance; panchayats are Article 40.

statements.t: The State takes steps to organise village panchayats under Article 40 of the Constitution.
The State takes steps to organise village panchayats under Article 42 of the Constitution.
statements.fact: Article 42 = just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief; panchayats are Article 40.

official_questions.rule: Arts 38-51 come in a run: 39 livelihood/equal pay, 39A legal aid, 40 panchayats, 41 work/assistance, 42 maternity, 43 living wage – expect neighbour swaps.

official_questions.stem: The Provincial Governments were given more powers under the system of Dyarchy by
options: The Government of India Act of 1909
The Government of India Act of 1919
official_questions.key: The Government of India Act of 1919
official_questions.core_fact: The GoI Act 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford) introduced dyarchy in the provinces (transferred and reserved subjects).

statements.t: Provincial governments were given more powers under dyarchy by Indian Councils Act of 1892.
statements.fact: 1892 Act enlarged councils, indirect election. Correct: Provincial governments were given more powers under dyarchy by The Government of India Act of 1919.

statements.t: Provincial governments were given more powers under dyarchy by The Government of India Act of 1909.
statements.d: The Government of India Act of 1909
statements.fact: 1909 Act: separate electorates. Correct: Provincial governments were given more powers under dyarchy by The Government of India Act of 1919.

statements.t: Provincial governments were given more powers under dyarchy by The Government of India Act of 1919.
statements.d: The Government of India Act of 1919

statements.t: Provincial governments were given more powers under dyarchy by The Gandhi-Irwin Pact.
statements.fact: Gandhi-Irwin Pact 1931 was an agreement, not an Act. Correct: Provincial governments were given more powers under dyarchy by The Government of India Act of 1919.

official_questions.rule: Dyarchy: provinces 1919; Centre proposed 1935 (never in force); provincial autonomy 1935.

official_questions.stem: Which Article of the Indian Constitution accords special status to Jammu and Kashmir?
official_questions.core_fact: Article 370 (Part XXI, temporary provisions) gave special status to Jammu and Kashmir; rendered inoperative by Presidential orders of 5-6 August 2019 (upheld by SC, Dec 2023).

statements.t: Article 365 of the Constitution accords special status to Jammu and Kashmir.
statements.fact: Article 365 = effect of a State's failure to comply with Union directions; J&K special status was Article 370.

statements.t: Article 370 of the Constitution accords special status to Jammu and Kashmir.
Article 380 of the Constitution accords special status to Jammu and Kashmir.
statements.fact: Article 380 (President's rule-making on officers) was repealed in 1956; special status was Article 370.

statements.t: Article 390 of the Constitution accords special status to Jammu and Kashmir.
statements.fact: There is no operative Article 390 on J&K (Part XXII ends at 395; 390 is not about J&K); special status was Article 370.

official_questions.rule: J&K = Art 370 (and 35A via 1954 order) – abrogated 2019; 371-371J = other States' special provisions (371J Hyderabad-Karnataka).
official_questions.key_note: Time-sensitive: true in 2008; since August 2019 Article 370 is inoperative and J&K is a Union Territory.

official_questions.stem: The 97th Constitutional Amendment Act resulted in the:
options: Prohibition of Members of Parliament to hold offices of profit
Increase in the number of languages in the 8th Schedule of the Constitution
Limiting the size of the cabinet at centre and state levels to 10 percent of the total strength of the respective lower houses
official_questions.key: Limiting the size of the cabinet at centre and state levels to 10 percent of the total strength of the respective lower houses
official_questions.core_fact: The Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment) Act 2003 (introduced as the 97th Amendment Bill) capped the Council of Ministers at 15% of the Lok Sabha/Assembly strength (min. 12 in States) and tightened anti-defection.

statements.t: The 97th Constitutional Amendment resulted in Readjustment of Lok Sabha Constituencies.
statements.fact: Delimitation freeze/readjustment was by the 84th (2001) and 87th (2003) Amendments.

statements.t: The 97th Constitutional Amendment resulted in Prohibition of Members of Parliament to hold offices of profit.
statements.fact: No amendment of that number prohibited offices of profit; disqualification is Art. 102 and the Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act 1959.

statements.t: The 97th Constitutional Amendment resulted in Increase in the number of languages in the 8th Schedule of the Constitution.
statements.fact: Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali were added to the 8th Schedule by the 92nd Amendment (2003).

statements.t: The 97th Constitutional Amendment resulted in Limiting the size of the cabinet at centre and state levels to 10 percent of the total strength of the respective lower houses.
statements.d: Limiting the size of the cabinet

official_questions.rule: Ministry cap = 91st Act 2003 (Bill 97) = 15%; the 97th Act (2011) is about co-operative societies (Part IXB).
official_questions.key_note: Key kept, but the keyed option is inaccurate twice: the cap is 15% (not 10%), and it is the 91st Amendment Act; the Constitution (97th Amendment) Act 2011 inserted Part IXB on co-operative societies.

statements.fact: Art. 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) makes free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14 a Fundamental Right; the RTE Act, 2009 brought it into force on 1 April 2010.

official_questions.stem: In which of the following points is Indian Constitution similar to that of America?
official_questions.core_fact: From the USA: Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independence of judiciary, impeachment of President, removal of judges, Vice-President as RS chairman. DPSP from Ireland; Rule of Law from Britain; India's Constitution is partly rigid, partly flexible (US is rigid).

statements.t: The Indian Constitution is similar to the American Constitution in Fundamental Rights.
The Indian Constitution is similar to the American Constitution in Directive principles of State Policy.
statements.fact: DPSP were borrowed from the Irish Constitution.

statements.t: The Indian Constitution is similar to the American Constitution in The Rule of Law.
statements.fact: Rule of Law comes from Britain (Dicey).

statements.t: The Indian Constitution is similar to the American Constitution in Rigidity of the Constitution.
statements.fact: The US Constitution is rigid; India's is a blend of rigidity and flexibility.

official_questions.rule: USA = FR, judicial review, impeachment, VP; UK = parliamentary govt, rule of law, single citizenship; Ireland = DPSP.

official_questions.stem: The Chairman of the Finance and Staff Committee of the Constituent Assembly of India was
official_questions.core_fact: Rajendra Prasad chaired the Finance and Staff Committee (also Rules of Procedure, Steering, National Flag ad hoc committees); Nehru chaired Union Powers, Union Constitution, States; Patel the Advisory Committee and Provincial Constitution; Ambedkar the Drafting Committee.

statements.t: The Chairman of the Finance and Staff Committee of the Constituent Assembly was Rajendra Prasad.
The Chairman of the Finance and Staff Committee of the Constituent Assembly was Jawaharlal Nehru.
statements.fact: Nehru chaired Union Powers/Union Constitution/States Committees.

statements.t: The Chairman of the Finance and Staff Committee of the Constituent Assembly was Vallabhbhai Patel.
statements.fact: Patel chaired the Advisory Committee on FR/minorities and Provincial Constitution Committee.

statements.t: The Chairman of the Finance and Staff Committee of the Constituent Assembly was B.R.Ambedkar.
statements.fact: Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee.

official_questions.rule: Prasad = Rules, Steering, Finance & Staff, Flag; Nehru = Union Powers/Constitution, States; Patel = Advisory, Provincial; Ambedkar = Drafting.

official_questions.stem: The Indian State that was given just the status of associate in 1974 and got the status of a full state in 1975 by the Amendments of the Constitution is
official_questions.core_fact: The 35th Amendment (1974) made Sikkim an 'associate State' (Art. 2A, Tenth Schedule); the 36th Amendment (1975) made it the 22nd full State (Art. 371F).

statements.t: Mizoram was made an associate State in 1974 and a full State in 1975 by constitutional amendments.
statements.fact: Mizoram became a State in 1987 (53rd Amendment).

statements.t: Manipur was made an associate State in 1974 and a full State in 1975 by constitutional amendments.
statements.fact: Manipur became a State in 1972 (NE Areas Reorganisation Act).

statements.t: Sikkim was made an associate State in 1974 and a full State in 1975 by constitutional amendments.
Tripura was made an associate State in 1974 and a full State in 1975 by constitutional amendments.
statements.fact: Tripura became a State in 1972.

official_questions.rule: Associate State = Sikkim only (35th, Art. 2A, 10th Schedule – later repealed); full State 36th, Art. 371F.

official_questions.stem: Which of the following is not a criterion for acquiring citizenship of India, subject to other conditions ?
official_questions.core_fact: The Citizenship Act 1955 provides five modes: birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory; ethnicity is not a mode.

statements.t: Naturalisation is a mode of acquiring Indian citizenship.
Birth is a mode of acquiring Indian citizenship.
Registration is a mode of acquiring Indian citizenship.
Ethnic identity is a mode of acquiring Indian citizenship.
statements.fact: Ethnic identity is not a mode; the modes are birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, incorporation of territory.

official_questions.rule: Citizenship modes: birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, incorporation – (CAA 2019 relaxes naturalisation, not a new mode).

official_questions.stem: The Constituent Assembly was composed roughly on the lines suggested by
official_questions.core_fact: The Constituent Assembly (1946) was constituted under the Cabinet Mission Plan: 389 seats (292 provinces, 93 princely states, 4 Chief Commissioners' provinces), indirectly elected by provincial assemblies.

statements.t: The Constituent Assembly was composed on the lines suggested by the Mountbatten.
statements.fact: Mountbatten's 3 June Plan (1947) partitioned the Assembly; it did not design its composition.

statements.t: The Constituent Assembly was composed on the lines suggested by the Cripps Mission.
statements.fact: Cripps (1942) proposed an elected constitution-making body, but it was rejected; the 1946 Assembly followed the Cabinet Mission.

statements.t: The Constituent Assembly was composed on the lines suggested by the Cabinet Mission.
The Constituent Assembly was composed on the lines suggested by the India Independence Act.
statements.fact: The Independence Act 1947 made the Assembly sovereign; it did not compose it.

official_questions.rule: 1942 Cripps offered, 1946 Cabinet Mission composed, 1947 Independence Act made sovereign.

official_questions.stem: Which of the following may be a violation of fundamental rights ?
options: Not allowing loudspeakers in a religious procession
official_questions.core_fact: In PUDR v UoI (1982) the SC held that paying less than the minimum wage is 'forced labour' under Article 23; reasonable restrictions under Art. 19(2)-(4) cover sovereignty/integrity and public order.

statements.t: Banning of a book may be a violation of fundamental rights.
statements.fact: A book can be banned as a reasonable restriction under Art. 19(2) (e.g. public order); per key it is not the violation.

statements.t: Not paying minimum wages may be a violation of fundamental rights.
Prohibition of secessionist activities may be a violation of fundamental rights.
statements.fact: Restrictions in the interest of sovereignty and integrity are expressly allowed (16th Amendment, Art. 19(2)-(4)).

statements.t: Not allowing loudspeakers in a religious procession may be a violation of fundamental rights.
statements.fact: Religious freedom (Art. 25) is subject to public order and health; loudspeaker limits are valid (Church of God 2000).

official_questions.rule: Below-minimum wage = forced labour (Art. 23, PUDR 1982); 19(2) grounds justify bans.
official_questions.key_note: 'May be' is loose: an arbitrary book ban could also violate Art. 19(1)(a). Key kept.

official_questions.stem:
Which of the following pairs is not correctly matched ?
(Event) — (Year)
official_questions.core_fact: Pitt's India Act 1784; Morley-Minto 1909; annulment 1911; Montford reforms = GoI Act 1919.

statements.t: The pair 'Pitt's India Act — 1784' is correctly matched.
The pair 'Morley-Minto Reforms — 1909' is correctly matched.
The pair 'Partition of Bengal annulled — 1911' is correctly matched.
The pair 'Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms — 1929' is correctly matched.
statements.fact: Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms = Government of India Act 1919.

official_questions.stem: The Objectives specified in the Preamble contain the basic structure of our Constitution. In this regard choose the correct answer :
options: The idea of basic structure is explained in the Constitution passed on 26th Jan 1950.
Basic structure means that which cannot be amended in exercise of the power under Article 368 of the Constitution.
Parliament is the supreme authority on the basic structure of our Constitution.
Courts have no jurisdiction on basic structure of Indian Constitution
official_questions.key: Basic structure means that which cannot be amended in exercise of the power under Article 368 of the Constitution.
official_questions.core_fact: The basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) means Parliament's amending power under Art. 368 cannot alter the Constitution's basic features; it is judge-made, not in the 1950 text, and courts decide what it covers.

statements.t: The idea of basic structure is explained in the Constitution passed on 26 January 1950.
statements.d: explained in the Constitution passed on 26th Jan 1950
statements.fact: The doctrine is judicial (1973); the 1950 text does not mention it.

statements.t: Basic structure means that which cannot be amended in exercise of the power under Article 368.
statements.d: cannot be amended in exercise of the power under Article 368

statements.t: Parliament is the supreme authority on the basic structure of the Constitution.
statements.fact: The judiciary, not Parliament, is the final authority on what is basic structure.

statements.t: Courts have no jurisdiction on the basic structure of the Constitution.
statements.fact: Courts alone determine and enforce the basic structure.

official_questions.rule: Basic structure: Kesavananda 1973 (13 judges, 7:6); courts decide content; Parliament's amending power limited.

official_questions.stem: Most important components of secularism are mentioned below, except
options: Prohibition against discrimination on ground of religion, caste, etc.
Sentiments of the majority of people towards cow and against its slaughter.
official_questions.core_fact: Indian secularism rests on equality (Art. 14), non-discrimination (Arts 15, 16), freedom of conscience for all persons including non-believers (Art. 25) and no State religion; cow protection is a DPSP (Art. 48) on agricultural grounds, not a component of secularism.

statements.t: Equality in Article 14 is a component of secularism.
Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, caste, etc. is a component of secularism.
statements.d: Prohibition against discrimination on ground of religion

statements.t: Sentiments of the majority towards the cow and against its slaughter are a component of secularism.
statements.fact: Cow protection is a DPSP (Art. 48: agriculture/animal husbandry), not a component of secularism.

statements.t: Secularism is not applicable to irreligious persons.
statements.fact: Secularism protects non-believers too (freedom of conscience, Art. 25).

official_questions.rule: Indian secularism = equal respect + freedom of conscience for all (incl. atheists); Art. 48 cow protection is DPSP, not secularism.
official_questions.key_note: Option 3 (majority sentiment on cow slaughter) is also not a component of secularism; the question has two exceptions. Final key (option 4) kept.

official_questions.stem: Social justice enables the Courts to uphold legislation, except
options: To provide a decent standard of living to the working people.
To protect the interest of the weaker sections of the society.
To enact unquestionable laws to protect certain people of the society.
official_questions.key: To enact unquestionable laws to protect certain people of the society.
official_questions.core_fact: Courts uphold social-justice laws that reduce economic inequality, secure a decent standard of living (Art. 43) and protect weaker sections (Art. 46); no law is immune from judicial review.

statements.t: Social justice enables courts to uphold legislation to remove economic inequalities.
Social justice enables courts to uphold legislation to provide a decent standard of living to working people.
Social justice enables courts to uphold legislation to protect the interests of weaker sections.
Social justice enables courts to uphold legislation that enacts unquestionable laws to protect certain people.
statements.fact: No law is 'unquestionable'; all are subject to judicial review (basic structure).

official_questions.rule: DPSP-based laws get a presumption of reasonableness, never immunity (except Art. 31C limits, read down in Minerva).

official_questions.stem: A person whose freedom of movement has been taken away by imprisonment or detention does not thereby lose his freedom of
official_questions.core_fact: A prisoner loses rights inconsistent with incarceration (movement, residence, profession) but keeps others such as freedom of expression (State of Maharashtra v Prabhakar Pandurang Sanzgiri 1966 – right to publish a book).

statements.t: A person whose movement is taken away by imprisonment does not thereby lose his freedom of Expression.
A person whose movement is taken away by imprisonment does not thereby lose his freedom of Profession.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked
statements.fact: Profession (19(1)(g)) is necessarily curtailed by imprisonment.

statements.t: A person whose movement is taken away by imprisonment does not thereby lose his freedom of Employment.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked
statements.fact: Employment outside prison is curtailed.

statements.t: A person whose movement is taken away by imprisonment does not thereby lose his freedom of Earning.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked
statements.fact: Earning a livelihood freely is curtailed.

official_questions.rule: Prisoner keeps expression, life/dignity (Sunil Batra); loses movement, residence, profession.

official_questions.stem: Regarding the Habeas Corpus, choose the wrong answer.
options: Habeas Corpus safeguards the liberty not only of the citizens but also of the persons within the territory.
Writ of Habeas Corpus is not to be entertained when a person is committed to judicial custody or public custody by the competent court.
A petition of Habeas Corpus lies against the executive authority, not available against the private individuals.
The Habeas Corpus petition cannot be dismissed on the ground of imperfect pleadings.
official_questions.key: A petition of Habeas Corpus lies against the executive authority, not available against the private individuals.
official_questions.core_fact: Habeas corpus protects any person (not only citizens), lies against public authorities and private individuals, is not issued where detention is by a competent court's order, and is not dismissed on technical defects in pleading.

statements.t: Habeas corpus safeguards the liberty of all persons within the territory, not only citizens.
Habeas corpus is not entertained when a person is committed to judicial custody by a competent court.
Habeas corpus lies only against the executive, not against private individuals.
statements.d: not available against the private individuals
statements.fact: Habeas corpus lies against both public authorities and private individuals.

statements.t: A habeas corpus petition cannot be dismissed on the ground of imperfect pleadings.

official_questions.rule: Habeas corpus vs both State and private; mandamus/certiorari/prohibition – not private persons; quo warranto – public office.

official_questions.stem: Regarding the Directive Principle of State Policy, choose the wrong answer.
options: Directive Principles have been held to supplement Fundamental Rights in achieving a Welfare State.
Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights for implementing the Directive Principles.
It shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.
Directive Principles do not confer any enforceable Rights and their alleged breach does not invalidate laws.
official_questions.key: Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights for implementing the Directive Principles.
official_questions.core_fact: DPSP supplement FR towards a welfare State; Art. 37: not enforceable but fundamental in governance and the State shall apply them in law-making; Parliament can amend FR to implement DPSP so long as basic structure is not violated.

statements.t: Directive Principles have been held to supplement Fundamental Rights in achieving a welfare State.
Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights for implementing the Directive Principles.
statements.fact: Parliament can amend FR to implement DPSP, subject to basic structure (Kesavananda, Minerva).

statements.t: It shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.
statements.d: duty of the State to apply

statements.t: Directive Principles confer no enforceable rights and their breach does not invalidate laws.
statements.d: do not confer any enforceable Rights

official_questions.rule: DPSP non-justiciable but fundamental; FR amendable for DPSP within basic structure (Art. 31C partly upheld).

official_questions.stem: The Preamble may be invoked to determine the ambit of
official_questions.core_fact: The Preamble is a key to the Constitution's interpretation; courts invoke it to determine the ambit of Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles (Kesavananda: part of the Constitution).

statements.t: The Preamble may be invoked to determine the ambit of Political welfare.
statements.fact: Not a constitutional category.

statements.t: The Preamble may be invoked to determine the ambit of People's demand.
statements.fact: Popular demands are not interpreted through the Preamble.

statements.t: The Preamble may be invoked to determine the ambit of States demand.
statements.fact: Not a constitutional category.

statements.t: The Preamble may be invoked to determine the ambit of Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.

official_questions.rule: Preamble: part of Constitution (Kesavananda), amendable within basic structure, non-justiciable, aids interpretation.

official_questions.stem: Regarding the Article 15 of the Constitution of India, find the wrong answer.
options: Article 15 is limited to citizens only.
Article 15 clause (1) and clause (2) both are limited to discrimination on grounds of religion, place of birth, etc.
Article 15 permits the State to make special provision for women and children.
Article 15 also permits the State to make any special provisions for SC, ST and socially and economically backward classes of citizens.
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 15 applies only to citizens; 15(1)-(2) bar discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth; 15(3) women and children; 15(4) socially and educationally backward classes, SC, ST; 15(6) (103rd, 2019) economically weaker sections.

statements.t: Article 15 is limited to citizens only.
Article 15(1) and (2) are limited to discrimination on grounds of religion, place of birth, etc.
Article 15 permits the State to make special provision for women and children.
statements.d: special provision for women and children

statements.t: Article 15 permits special provisions for SC, ST and socially and economically backward classes.
statements.fact: Art. 15(4) says 'socially and educationally backward classes'; economic criterion appears only for EWS (15(6), 2019).

official_questions.rule: SEBC = socially AND educationally (Arts 15(4), 340); EWS = economic (15(6), 16(6)).
official_questions.key_note: Deleted by APPSC; the 'wrong answer' is arguably option 4 (economically vs educationally), but the 103rd Amendment's EWS clause made it ambiguous.

official_questions.stem: Which of the following are not the federal features of the Indian Constitution ?
official_questions.core_fact: Federal features: written and rigid Constitution, dual polity, division of powers, independent judiciary, bicameralism; unitary features: strong Centre, single citizenship, Centre-appointed Governor, emergency provisions, all-India services.

statements.t: A rigid Constitution is a federal feature of the Indian Constitution.
Bicameral legislature is a federal feature.
Independent judiciary is a federal feature.
The office of the Governor is a federal feature.
statements.fact: The Centre-appointed Governor is a unitary feature.

official_questions.rule: Unitary: Governor, single citizenship, emergencies, integrated judiciary, AIS, Art. 3 changes.

official_questions.stem: What option does the government exercise and legislators have when they do not like a decision made by the Supreme Court ?
options: Pass a law challenging the decision
Pass a constitutional amendment that circumvents the decision
Both are options, pass a constitutional amendment that circumvents the decision or pass a law challenging the decision
No options are there before the legislators and executives
official_questions.key: Both are options, pass a constitutional amendment that circumvents the decision or pass a law challenging the decision
official_questions.core_fact: Legislatures may nullify a judgment by removing its basis through an amendment of the Constitution (e.g. 1st Amendment after Champakam) or a validating law that cures the defect (e.g. SC/ST Atrocities Amendment 2018); they cannot simply overrule a judgment.

statements.t: When the government and legislators do not like a Supreme Court decision, they may: Pass a law challenging the decision.
statements.d: Pass a law challenging the decision
statements.fact: Only one of the two available routes.

statements.t: When the government and legislators do not like a Supreme Court decision, they may: Pass a constitutional amendment that circumvents the decision.
statements.fact: Only one of the two routes.

statements.t: When the government and legislators do not like a Supreme Court decision, they may: Both are options, pass a constitutional amendment that circumvents the decision or pass a law challenging the decision.
When the government and legislators do not like a Supreme Court decision, they may: No options are there before the legislators and executives.
statements.fact: Both legislative routes exist.

official_questions.rule: Overriding judgments: amend Constitution (e.g. 1st, 24th, 99th) or validating law – subject to basic structure.

official_questions.stem: Which of the following Liberties is sought to be secured to the citizens of India in the Preamble ?
options: Thought, expression, belief, faith and worship
official_questions.key: Thought, expression, belief, faith and worship
official_questions.core_fact: The Preamble secures 'LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship'.

statements.t: The Preamble secures liberty of Thought, expression, belief, faith and worship.
statements.d: Thought, expression, belief, faith and worship

statements.t: The Preamble secures liberty of Thought, expression, belief and faith.
statements.fact: 'worship' omitted.

statements.t: The Preamble secures liberty of Expression, belief, faith and worship.
statements.fact: 'thought' omitted.

statements.t: The Preamble secures liberty of Thought, expression, faith and worship.
statements.fact: 'belief' omitted.

official_questions.rule: Preamble: Justice (social, economic, political) – Liberty (thought, expression, belief, faith, worship) – Equality (status, opportunity) – Fraternity (dignity, unity and integrity).

official_questions.stem: Due to the existence of which article, the State cannot interfere and dispossess a person's property except in accordance with the procedure established by law ?
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 300A (44th Amendment 1978): no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.

statements.t: Because of Article 300, the State cannot dispossess a person of property except by law.
statements.fact: Art. 300 concerns suits by and against the Government; property protection is 300A.

statements.t: Because of Article 330A, the State cannot dispossess a person of property except by law.
statements.fact: Art. 330A (2023) reserves seats for women in Lok Sabha; property is 300A.

statements.t: Because of Article 299, the State cannot dispossess a person of property except by law.
statements.fact: Art. 299 concerns government contracts.

statements.t: Because of Article 299A, the State cannot dispossess a person of property except by law.
statements.fact: There is no Article 299A.

official_questions.rule: Property: Art. 19(1)(f), 31 deleted (44th) -> Art. 300A (Part XII, legal right).
official_questions.key_note: Deleted by APPSC: the correct provision (Article 300A) is not among the options.

official_questions.stem: To provide reservations to economically weaker sections, the Lok Sabha has passed the following amendment bill.
official_questions.core_fact: The Constitution (124th Amendment) Bill, 2019 (passed by Lok Sabha 8 Jan 2019) became the Constitution (103rd Amendment) Act, 2019, inserting Arts. 15(6) and 16(6) for up to 10% EWS reservation (upheld in Janhit Abhiyan, 2022).

statements.t: To provide reservation to economically weaker sections the Lok Sabha passed the 136th Constitutional Amendment Bill.
statements.fact: The Constitution (124th Amendment) Bill, 2019 (passed by Lok Sabha 8 Jan 2019) became the Constitution (103rd Amendment) Act, 2019, inserting Arts. 15(6) and 16(6) for up to 10% EWS reservation (upheld in Janhit Abhiyan, 2022).

statements.t: To provide reservation to economically weaker sections the Lok Sabha passed the 124th Constitutional Amendment Bill.
To provide reservation to economically weaker sections the Lok Sabha passed the 128th Constitutional Amendment Bill.

official_questions.stem: Which of the following Amendment(s) provide(s) for reservation in jobs and admissions ?
official_questions.core_fact: 77th (1995): Art. 16(4A) reservation in promotion for SC/ST; 81st (2000): Art. 16(4B) carry-forward of unfilled vacancies; 82nd (2000): proviso to Art. 335 relaxing qualifying marks in promotion; reservation in admissions came by the 93rd (2005, Art. 15(5)).

statements.t: The 77th Amendment provides for reservation (in promotion) in jobs.
The 82nd Amendment provides for reservation-related relaxation in jobs.
The 81st Amendment provides for reservation (carry-forward backlog) in jobs.

official_questions.rule: Jobs: 77th (promotion), 81st (backlog), 82nd (relaxation), 85th (consequential seniority); admissions: 93rd (15(5)); EWS: 103rd.

official_questions.stem:
Which of the following are among the Fundamental Duties of citizens laid down in the Indian Constitution ?
I. To protect the weaker sections from social injustice.
II. To develop scientific temper and spirit of inquiry.
III. To preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture.
IV. To safeguard public property and adjure violence.
Which of the statements given above are correct ?
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 51A: (f) preserve heritage of composite culture, (h) scientific temper, (i) safeguard public property and abjure violence; protecting weaker sections from social injustice is DPSP Art. 46.

statements.t: Protecting the weaker sections from social injustice is a Fundamental Duty.
statements.fact: Protection of weaker sections from social injustice is a DPSP (Art. 46).

statements.t: Developing scientific temper and spirit of inquiry is a Fundamental Duty.
Preserving the rich heritage of our composite culture is a Fundamental Duty.
Safeguarding public property and abjuring violence is a Fundamental Duty.

official_questions.rule: FD (51A) duties of citizens; Art. 46 = State's duty to weaker sections – watch DPSP/FD swaps.

official_questions.stem:
The Constitution confers which of the following Articles that denies the rights to aliens (Foreign Citizens) ?
I. Articles 29 and 30
II. Article 19
III. Articles 23 and 24
IV. Article 16
Choose the correct answer using the codes given below :
official_questions.core_fact: Citizens only: Arts 15, 16, 19, 29, 30; all persons (incl. foreigners): Arts 14, 20, 21, 21A, 22, 23, 24, 25-28.

statements.t: Articles 29 and 30 are denied to aliens.
Article 19 is denied to aliens.
Articles 23 and 24 are denied to aliens.
statements.fact: Arts 23 and 24 protect all persons, including foreigners.

statements.t: Article 16 is denied to aliens.

official_questions.rule: Citizen-only FR: 15, 16, 19, 29, 30 – everything else is for all persons (enemy aliens excluded from Art. 22 protection).

official_questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
I. The Preamble was enacted before the enactment of the entire Constitution.
II. The Preamble is a part of the Constitution but has no legal effect independently of other parts.
III. It is enforceble through Courts of Law.
IV. The Objectives Resolution by Jawaharlal Nehru finally became the foundation for the Preamble.
Which of the statements given above are incorrect ?
official_questions.core_fact: The Preamble was enacted after the rest of the Constitution (to conform to it); it is part of the Constitution (Kesavananda) but non-justiciable and has no independent legal effect; it is based on Nehru's Objectives Resolution (13 Dec 1946, adopted 22 Jan 1947).

statements.t: The Preamble was enacted before the enactment of the entire Constitution.
statements.fact: The Preamble was enacted last, after the rest of the Constitution.

statements.t: The Preamble is part of the Constitution but has no legal effect independently of other parts.
The Preamble is enforceable through courts of law.
statements.fact: The Preamble is not enforceable in courts.

statements.t: Nehru's Objectives Resolution became the foundation of the Preamble.

official_questions.rule: Preamble: enacted last, part of Constitution (1973), non-justiciable, amended once (42nd: socialist, secular, integrity).

official_questions.stem: With child labour being made illegal and right to education becoming a fundamental right for children, this right against exploitation has become more meaningful. Which of the following pairs of Articles provide for right to education and prohibition of child labour respectively ?
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 21A (86th Amendment 2002): free and compulsory education for 6-14; Art. 24: no child below 14 in factories, mines or hazardous employment; Art. 23: traffic and forced labour.

statements.t: Articles 21A and 23 provide for right to education and prohibition of child labour respectively.
statements.fact: Art. 23 is traffic/forced labour; child labour is Art. 24.

statements.t: Articles 21A and 24 provide for right to education and prohibition of child labour respectively.
Articles 23 and 24 provide for right to education and prohibition of child labour respectively.
statements.fact: Art. 23 is not education.

statements.t: Articles 14 and 19 provide for right to education and prohibition of child labour respectively.
statements.fact: Arts 14 and 19 are equality and freedoms.

official_questions.rule: 21A education (6-14), 24 child labour (<14 in hazardous), 45 ECCE (<6), 51A(k) parents' duty.

official_questions.stem:
With reference to the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements :
I. It was intended to protect Central and State laws that are included in it from judicial review on the ground of violation of Fundamental rights.
II. The entries included in it are not restricted to the subject of land reforms and abolition of the zamindari system alone.
III. Article 31B carries a retrospective effect but it has ceased to be operative after the 'I.R. Coelho Case' (2007).
IV. The entries incorporated in it are only done so, by the power of the Central Government.
Which of the statements given above are correct ?
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 31B (1st Amendment 1951) shields Ninth Schedule laws (Central and State) from FR challenge, retrospectively; entries now cover reservation, industry etc. (284 laws); I.R. Coelho (2007): laws added after 24 Apr 1973 are reviewable on basic structure – 31B remains operative; entries are added only by Parliament through constitutional amendment.

statements.t: The Ninth Schedule protects Central and State laws in it from judicial review on FR grounds.
Ninth Schedule entries are not restricted to land reforms and zamindari abolition.
Article 31B is retrospective but ceased to be operative after I.R. Coelho (2007).
statements.fact: 31B is retrospective, but it remains operative; Coelho only opened post-1973 entries to basic-structure review.

statements.t: Entries are incorporated in the Ninth Schedule only by the power of the Central Government.
statements.fact: Entries are added by Parliament through constitutional amendment, not by the Central Government.

official_questions.rule: 9th Schedule: 1st Amendment 1951; Coelho 2007: post-24.4.1973 laws open to basic-structure test; TN 69% reservation law (76th Amendment) is there.

official_questions.stem:
The 'Territory of India' and the 'Union of India' are two distinct and different expressions due to which of the following reason/reasons ?
I. The 'Union of India' includes just States and Union Territories while the 'Territory of India' includes in addition to States and Union Territories, those territories that may be acquired by the Government of India at any future time as well.
II. The expression 'Union of India' is mentioned in the Constitution of India, but the expression 'Territory of India' is not found in the Constitution of India.
III. The First Schedule of the Constitution of India is with reference to just the 'Union of India' but not the 'Territory of India'.
IV. The Union Territories are covered by the expression 'Territory of India' and not by the expression 'Union of India'.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below :
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 1: India is a Union of States; Union of India = States only; Territory of India = States + UTs + acquired territories; both expressions are in Art. 1; First Schedule lists States and UTs.

statements.t: The Union of India includes States and UTs, while the Territory of India also includes acquired territories.
statements.d: includes just States and Union Territories
statements.fact: The Union of India includes only the States, not UTs.

statements.t: 'Union of India' is in the Constitution but 'Territory of India' is not.
statements.fact: Both expressions occur in Art. 1.

statements.t: The First Schedule refers only to the Union of India and not the Territory of India.
statements.fact: The First Schedule lists States and UTs, i.e. the territory, not only the Union.

statements.t: UTs are covered by 'Territory of India' and not by 'Union of India'.
statements.d: covered by ... 'Territory of India' and not ... 'Union of India'

official_questions.rule: Union of India = States (federal partners); Territory of India = States + UTs + acquired.

official_questions.stem:
With reference to Indian polity, which one of the following statements would you accept as appropriate ideas referring to 'Equality' ?
I. The primacy of equality is safeguarded, defined and enforced by the courts of law rather than by the Constitution as conceptualized by A.V. Dicey.
II. Article 14 of the Constitution of India constitutes only the concept of 'Equality before the law' but does not mention the concept of 'Equal Protection of Laws'.
III. Article 194 and Article 361A of the Constitution of India are indicative of the fact that equality in India is not absolute.
IV. The theory of equality includes distinction of merit but not distinction on account of hereditary titles or nobility as propounded by the Balaji Raghavan Case (1995).
Select the correct answer using the codes given below :
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 14 has both 'equality before law' (British) and 'equal protection of laws' (American); Dicey's rule of law – rights flow from courts' judgments in Britain (in India the Constitution is the source); exceptions to equality include legislative privileges (Art. 194) and immunity for reporting proceedings (Art. 361A); Balaji Raghavan (1995): awards for merit are not titles.

statements.t: Primacy of equality is safeguarded, defined and enforced by courts rather than by the Constitution, as conceptualised by Dicey.
statements.d: by the courts of law rather than by the Constitution
statements.fact: Dicey's court-made primacy fits Britain; in India equality is defined by the Constitution itself.

statements.t: Article 14 contains only 'equality before the law' and not 'equal protection of laws'.
statements.d: does not mention ... 'Equal Protection of Laws'
statements.fact: Art. 14 includes both concepts.

statements.t: Articles 194 and 361A show that equality in India is not absolute.
Equality includes distinction of merit but not hereditary titles, as held in Balaji Raghavan (1995).

official_questions.rule: Art. 14 exceptions: 361 (President/Governor), 105/194 (privileges), 361A, 31C, diplomatic immunity; awards ≠ titles (Balaji Raghavan).

official_questions.stem:
Which of the following statement/statements is/are correct with regard to the Fundamental Duties ?
I. Fundamental Duties are confined to just the citizens of India with the exception of Article 51A(i), which is also applicable to foreigners that are resident in India.
II. The Verma Committee on Fundamental Duties of the Citizens (1999) had recommended the implementation of the Fundamental Duties irrespective of the existence of legal provisions.
III. In 'Kesavananda Bharati' Case (1973), the Supreme Court of India held that the Fundamental Duties may be used to decide the constitutionality of laws that are otherwise ambiguous to interpret.
IV. The Sardar Swaran Singh Committee had recommended for penalties to be considered in the eventuality of non-compliance of any of the Fundamental Duties.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below :
official_questions.core_fact: FD (Art. 51A, 42nd Amendment 1976) apply to citizens only; Verma Committee (1999) identified existing legal provisions for some duties; Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommended penalties for non-compliance; Kesavananda (1973) predates FD.

statements.t: FD are confined to citizens except Art. 51A(i), which also applies to resident foreigners.
statements.fact: All FD are confined to citizens; none extends to foreigners.

statements.t: The Verma Committee (1999) recommended implementing FD irrespective of legal provisions.
statements.d: irrespective of the existence of legal provisions
statements.fact: Verma Committee identified existing legal provisions to implement some duties, not implementation irrespective of law.

statements.t: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973) the SC held FD may be used to decide constitutionality of ambiguous laws.
statements.fact: FD were added in 1976, after Kesavananda (1973); the interpretive use was held later (e.g. AIIMS Students Union 2001).

statements.t: The Swaran Singh Committee recommended penalties for non-compliance with FD.

official_questions.rule: FD: Swaran Singh 1976 (8 duties proposed, 10 added), 11th by 86th (2002); citizens only; Verma 1999.

official_questions.stem:
With regards to Directive Principles of State Policy, what is the correct chronological order in which the following additions/changes were incorporated into the Constitution of India through amendments ?
I. The adding of a second aspect relating to Article 38.
II. The changing of the subject-matter of Article 45.
III. The adding of Article 43B.
IV. The adding of Article 48A.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below :
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 48A by 42nd (1976); Art. 38(2) by 44th (1978); Art. 45 substituted by 86th (2002); Art. 43B by 97th (2011).

statements.t: Art. 48A (1976) was added before Art. 38(2) (1978).
Art. 38(2) (1978) came before Art. 45 was changed (2002).
Art. 45 change (2002) came before Art. 43B (2011).
Art. 38(2) was added before Art. 48A (order I, IV, II, III).
statements.fact: Art. 48A (42nd) preceded Art. 38(2) (44th); order I, IV, II, III reverses them.

official_questions.rule: DPSP additions: 42nd – 39(f), 39A, 43A, 48A; 44th – 38(2); 86th – 45; 97th – 43B.

official_questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
I. The 25th Constitutional Amendment Act (1971) inserted a new Article 31C, whose first provision was declared as invalid by the Supreme Court in the Keshavananda Bharati Case (1973).
II. The Supreme Court in the Minerva Mills Case (1980) considered the extension of the scope of the second provision of Article 31C as invalid as well.
III. The Supreme Court in the Minerva Mills Case (1980) has considered the importance of harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.
IV. The present interpretation with respect to the Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is the same reiteration of the principle that was first propounded by the Supreme Court in the Chamapakan Dorairajan case (1951).
Which of the statement/statements given above is/are incorrect ?
official_questions.core_fact: 25th Amendment (1971) inserted Art. 31C; Kesavananda (1973) struck down its second provision (no judicial review); 42nd (1976) extended the first provision to all DPSP – struck down in Minerva Mills (1980), which stressed harmony and balance between FR and DPSP; Champakam Dorairajan (1951) held FR prevail over DPSP – no longer the rule.

statements.t: Kesavananda invalidated the first provision of Art. 31C inserted by the 25th Amendment.
statements.fact: Kesavananda invalidated the second provision (bar on judicial review), not the first.

statements.t: Minerva Mills held the extension of the second provision of Art. 31C invalid as well.
statements.fact: Minerva struck down the 42nd Amendment's extension of the first provision (to all DPSP), not of the second.

statements.t: Minerva Mills stressed harmony and balance between FR and DPSP.
The present FR-DPSP interpretation reiterates the principle of Champakam Dorairajan (1951).
statements.fact: Champakam (1951) held FR superior to DPSP; the present view is harmony (Minerva).

official_questions.rule: 31C: 1st provision (39(b),(c) laws immune from 14, 19) – valid; 2nd provision (no court review) – struck (Kesavananda); 42nd extension – struck (Minerva).
official_questions.key_note: Initial key only. The stem asks for 'incorrect' statements, but the keyed 'Only III' fits only a 'correct' reading: on the facts III is the one true statement and I, II, IV are false (incorrect set = option 'I, II and IV'). Key kept; truths given on the facts.

official_questions.stem:
With reference to the procedure for Amendment of the Constitution, consider the following statements :
I. A private member of the House of the Parliament can introduce the Bill for amendment of the Constitution only after the prior permission of the President.
II. Article 368 of the Constitution of India provides for three types of amendments - simple majority, special majority and ratification of half of the States by a simple majority.
III. For amendments that require ratification of half the States by a simple majority, it is not necessary that all the State Legislatures must take action on the Bill.
IV. The State Legislatures can pass a resolution requesting the Parliament to amend Article 368 in the same manner, as it could be done for the creation or abolition of Legislative Councils in the States.
Which of the statement/statements given above is/are correct ?
official_questions.core_fact: Amendment bill may be introduced by a minister or private member without President's prior permission; Art. 368 itself provides special majority and special majority + ratification by half the States (simple-majority amendments are outside 368); ratification by half suffices – others need not act; States cannot initiate amendments (Art. 169 resolution is for councils only).

statements.t: A private member can introduce a constitutional amendment bill only after the President's prior permission.
statements.d: only after the prior permission of the President
statements.fact: No prior permission of the President is needed.

statements.t: Art. 368 provides for three types of amendment – simple majority, special majority and ratification.
statements.fact: Art. 368 provides only two methods; simple-majority changes are 'not amendments under 368'.

statements.t: For amendments needing ratification by half the States, all States need not act on the bill.
statements.d: not necessary that all the State Legislatures

statements.t: State legislatures can request Parliament to amend Art. 368 like for creating/abolishing Councils.
statements.d: request the Parliament to amend Article 368
statements.fact: States cannot initiate amendments of Art. 368; the Art. 169 route applies only to Legislative Councils.

official_questions.rule: Art. 368: either House, minister or private member, no President's prior sanction, no joint sitting, President must assent (24th).

official_questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution :
I. The doctrine of the 'Basic Structure' has been incorporated into the Constitution of India by an Act of Parliament.
II. Presently, the Parliament under Article 368 of the Constitution of India can amend any part of the Constitution without affecting the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution.
III. Parliament's limited power to amend the Constitution is also an element of the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution.
IV. The Supreme Court in the 'Kumar Padma Prasad Case' (1992) has declared that the mandate to build a 'welfare state' is an element of the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above are correct ?
official_questions.core_fact: Basic structure is judge-made (Kesavananda 1973), not enacted; Parliament can amend any part without destroying it; limited amending power is itself basic structure (Minerva Mills 1980); welfare State was listed in Minerva/Indra Sawhney contexts – Kumar Padma Prasad (1992) was on independence of judiciary (judge's qualification).

statements.t: The basic structure doctrine has been incorporated by an Act of Parliament.
statements.fact: The doctrine is judicial, not incorporated by any Act.

statements.t: Parliament under Art. 368 can amend any part of the Constitution without affecting the basic structure.
statements.d: can amend any part ... without affecting the 'Basic Structure'

statements.t: Parliament's limited power to amend is an element of the basic structure.
Kumar Padma Prasad (1992) declared the welfare-State mandate an element of the basic structure.
statements.fact: Kumar Padma Prasad (1992) concerned independence of the judiciary; welfare State was recognised in other cases (Minerva Mills).

official_questions.rule: Basic structure elements and cases: limited amending power (Minerva), judicial review (Minerva/L. Chandra Kumar), secularism/federalism (Bommai), free and fair elections (Indira Gandhi 1975), independence of judiciary (Kumar Padma Prasad).

official_questions.stem:
Which of the following statement/statements is/are valid with respect to the Preamble of the Indian Constitution ?
I. The term 'democratic' as used in the Preamble is a mix of British Fabian Socialism and American Populism.
II. The term 'Republic' in the Preamble indicates that India has an elected head, called the Prime Minister.
III. The 'Liberty' expressed in the Preamble is neither absolute nor qualified.
IV. The term 'Fraternity' as used by the Preamble, originally denoted the dignity of the individual only.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below :
official_questions.core_fact: 'Democratic' = political, social and economic democracy (representative, parliamentary); 'Republic' = elected head of State (President); liberty is qualified (reasonable restrictions); fraternity originally assured 'the dignity of the individual and the unity of the Nation' (integrity added 1976).

statements.t: 'Democratic' in the Preamble is a mix of British Fabian Socialism and American Populism.
statements.d: British Fabian Socialism and American Populism
statements.fact: Fabian socialism/populism describe Indian 'socialism' discussions, not 'democratic'.

statements.t: 'Republic' means India has an elected head called the Prime Minister.
statements.fact: Republic = elected head of State, the President (not the PM).

statements.t: Liberty in the Preamble is neither absolute nor qualified.
statements.fact: Liberty in the Preamble is qualified (not absolute).

statements.t: Fraternity originally denoted the dignity of the individual only.
statements.fact: Fraternity originally assured both dignity of the individual and unity of the Nation.

official_questions.rule: Preamble: Republic = elected President; liberty qualified; fraternity = dignity + unity (+ integrity, 1976).
